many users to train a centralized ML model such as deep neural networks [1]–[4]. It finds broad applications such
as improving query suggestion accuracy in Google virtual keyboard [5], on-device speech processing for Amazon

model and sends it back to the users. A new round of local training will be performed by the users using the

to the inputs, i.e., they should infer absolutely nothing about the input set. Given that the server and each relay
can respectively collude with at most T users, the optimal rate region, which consists of communication rates
over the two network layers and the secret key rates, has been characterized. A core insight from [37] is that
the mixing (i.e., summation) of the users’ uploaded messages at the relays makes it harder for the server to infer
the inputs which results in a smaller source key rate than in the original star network considered by Zhao &
Sun [13]. HSA has also been studied in a similar network architecture but with different communication protocols
and security models [39]–[41]. Specifically, these work relies on inter-relay communication and focuses solely on
communication rate, which is different from [37] which requires no communication among relays and studies both
communication and key rates.
One notable limitation of the network model considered in [37] is that each user is associated with only one relay,
which may not be general in practice. This simple single-association pattern also limits the coding opportunities
across relays, restricting the potential for more efficient communication and secret key reuse among the outgoing
links of each user. In this paper, we study HSA with a more general cyclic user-relay association pattern as
shown in Fig. 1. The system consists of K users and K relays where each user is associated with B consecutive
relays in a cyclic wrap-around manner.1 The aggregation process consists of two hops. In the first hop, each
user sends a message to each of its associated relays. In the second hop, upon receiving the messages from its
associated users, each relay generates and sends a message to the server. The server aims to recover the sum
of inputs of all users subject to server and relay security constraints whose definitions are consistent with that
of [37]. We aim to find the optimal rate region R∗, which is defined as the closure of all achievable tuples
(RX, RY , RZ, RZΣ) where RX, RY , RZ and RZΣ denotes respectively the per-user upload communication rate,
per-relay upload communication rate, the individual key rate, and the source key rate (i.e., the total number
of independent key symbols contained in all users’ individual keys). Our major finding is that there exists a
fundamental trade-off between the association number B and the communication and key rates: the larger B is,
the smaller the optimal communication and key rates are. More specifically, when B ≤K −1, we characterize
the optimal rate region which shows that to securely compute one symbol of the desired input sum, each user
needs to send at least RX = 1 symbol to the associated relays, each relay needs to send at RY = 1/B symbols

D. Summary of Contributions
The major contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
• We present an information-theoretic formulation of HSA with cyclic wrap-around association with the
consideration of both server and relay security. We study both the communication and key generation
performance under a two-hop communication protocol. For an important regime B ≤K −1, the optimal
rate region is fully characterized and a fundamental trade-off between the association number B and the
communication and key rates is identified.
• We propose a secure aggregation scheme which consists of a linear key generation scheme and a communi-
cation scheme for input aggregation. Given the source key, the individual keys of the users are generated as
linear combinations of the source key symbols. The proposed input aggregation scheme efficiently exploits the
inter-relay coding opportunities, i.e., coding across different inputs and the symbols of each input, to reduce
the relay-to-server communication rate. The linear coefficients for the individual keys are then designed
accordingly such that the server and relay security constraints can be satisfied.
• We present a novel entropic converse proof and derive lower bounds on the achievable communication and
key rates for any B ≤K. In particular, we show that RX ≥1, RY ≥max{1/B, 1/(K −1)}, RZ ≥1/B
and RZΣ ≥max{1, K/B −1} for any B ≤K. When B ≤K −1, the derived bounds match the achievable
rates so that the optimal rate region can be established. When B = K, the scheme for B = K −1 can
be applied by letting each user send an empty message over the last outgoing link (equivalent to disabling
the link) so that each user effectively connects to K −1 relays. This results in the achievable rate tuple of
(RX = 1, RY = 1/(K −1), RZ = 1/(K −1), RZΣ = 1). Comparing with the converse bounds, we see that
despite RZ is within a factor of at most 1 + 1/(K −1) ≤2 to its optimum, the achievable rates RX, RY
and RZΣ all reach their individually minimum. As an intriguing discussion, we prove the impossibility
of (RX = 1, RY = 1, RZ = 1/2, RZΣ = 1) using the example of B = K = 2, which sheds light on
understanding the optimal solution for general K where B = K.

We notice that the scheme for the cases of B ∈[K −1] described in the previous section cannot be generalized
to the case of B = K to achieve RX = 1, RY = 1/(K −1), RZ = 1/K and RZΣ = 111 simultaneously.
However, we can apply the scheme for B = K −1 by disabling the last outgoing link from each user. This
scheme gives an achievable rate tuple of (1, 1/(K −1), 1/(K −1), 1). Compared with the converse bounds
RX ≥1, RY ≥1/(K −1), RZ ≥1/K and RZΣ ≥1 derived in Section VI, we see that the communication and
source key rates reach their minimum, while the individual key rate is at most K/(K −1) ≤2 times from its
optima. This means that we only experience a constant-factor loss in the individual key rate by directly applying
the existing scheme for B = K −1. In Section VII-A, we provide an insightful discussion on the impossibility
of RZ = 1/2 using the example of B = K = 2. It is conjectured that when B = K, ∀K ≥3, the rate tuple
(1, 1/(K −1), 1/K, 1) is not achievable. We leave the proof of this conjecture and the derivation of the optimal
solution for B = K as future work.

VII. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we studied secure aggregation in a hierarchical network with cyclic wrap-around association, where
users connect to the aggregation server through an intermediate layer of relays. A fundamental trade-off between the
association number B and the communication and key rates was identified. More specifically, when B ≤K −1, the

27
optimal rate region has been completely characterized which shows that the optimal relay-to-server communication
rate and the individual key rate are inversely proportional to B, the optimal user-to-relay communication stays
constant, and the source key rate is also inversely proportional to B but does not go below one. Compared to the
existing single-association HSA, multiple association allows each user to distribute its input to multiple relays and
creates coding opportunities for improving the communication and key rates. Without the security requirements,
this coding opportunity has been demonstrated in the context of communication-efficient gradient coding (GC) [46].
Our results showed that when B ≤K −1, the same relay-to-server communication rate as GC can be achieved
with a nontrivial security key design, implying that security does not incur additional communication overhead.
However, when B = K, the optimal relay-to-server communication rate cannot be reduced beyond 1/(K −1)
which is strictly larger than 1/K in GC, indicating a cost in communication rates due to security. To summarize,
we characterized the optimal rate region for any B ≤K −1 and provided an achievable scheme for the case of
B = K. In the following, we present an interesting observation that RZ = 1/2 is not achievable for B = K = 2,
which implies that the proposed converse bound RZ ≥1/B in Section VI-C might not be achievable for general
K when B = K.
